title: Why does a naive `if (!alreadyProcessed(id)) { process(); markProcessed(id); }` dedup still double-process under concurrency or on crash, and what are the two fixes: make the dedup write atomic (`INSERT ... ` with a `UNIQUE(event_id)` constraint so only one consumer wins) and commit the business update and the dedup record in the SAME database transaction (so a crash after the update but before marking cannot cause reprocessing to re-apply it)?
shortTitle: Why does a naive `if (!alreadyProcessed(id)) { process(); markProcessed(id); }` dedup still double-process
keyPoints: The naive check-then-act dedup has a race window under concurrency and a crash window between process and mark
Concurrency: two consumers both read not-processed, both process, because the check and mark are separate
Crash: consumer processes but crashes before marking, so redelivery finds the ID unmarked and reprocesses
Fix 1: atomic INSERT with UNIQUE constraint so only one consumer can win the claim
Fix 2: commit the business change and the dedup record in the same database transaction
The two fixes are complementary: unique constraint handles concurrency, same transaction handles crashes
Reordering the three lines does not fix it; the problem is lack of atomicity

s1_definition.oneliner: Naive dedup double-processes because the check and the mark are separate, racing under concurrency and losing the mark on crash, so you make the mark an atomic unique insert and commit it in the same transaction as the business change.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Race window** – two consumers both call `alreadyProcessed(id)`, both see false, both process, because the gap between check and mark is not atomic.
- **Crash window** – a consumer processes but crashes before `markProcessed(id)`, so the ID is never marked and redelivery reprocesses.
- **Fix 1: atomic claim** – INSERT with a UNIQUE constraint on event_id so only one consumer wins.
- **Fix 2: same transaction** – the business change and the dedup record commit together, so a crash cannot separate them.
- **Complementary** – the unique constraint handles concurrency; the same transaction handles crashes.
s1_definition.analogy: Two clerks at National Bank of India both glance at the logbook, both see the instruction number is not logged yet, and both credit Priya, because the glance and the pen-stroke were separate actions with a gap. Separately, one clerk credits Priya but faints before writing the number in the logbook, so when the instruction comes again it looks brand new. The fix is a logbook that physically allows each number to be written only once, and doing the credit and the logbook entry as one inseparable action.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  NAIVE (BROKEN):
  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
  │ Check    │  │ Process  │  │ Mark     │
  │ (READ)   │  │ (EFFECT) │  │ (WRITE)  │
  └─────┬────┘  └─────┬────┘  └──────────┘
        │ race        │ crash
        │ window      │ window
        ▼             ▼

  FIXED:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          Same Transaction                 │
  │                                           │
  │  ┌───────────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐ │
  │  │ INSERT inbox      │  │ Credit Priya │ │
  │  │ UNIQUE(event_id)  │  │ 50000.00     │ │
  │  │ (atomic claim)    │  │              │ │
  │  └───────────────────┘  └──────────────┘ │
  │                                           │
  │  COMMIT: both or neither                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Concurrency: UNIQUE rejects second INSERT -> only one wins
  Crash before COMMIT: nothing happened -> redelivery safe
  Crash after COMMIT: both present -> duplicate detected
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The naive check-then-act dedup fails because its three operations, read, side effect, and write, are not atomic. Under concurrency, two consumers both pass the check because neither has marked yet, so both process. On crash, the consumer processes but the mark is never written, so redelivery reprocesses. Reordering the lines moves the bug but does not eliminate it; the fix is atomicity.

Fix 1 makes the claim atomic with a UNIQUE constraint on event_id, so only one consumer can win the INSERT and the concurrent loser gets a duplicate-key error. Fix 2 commits the business change and the inbox record in the same database transaction, so the only outcomes are both present or neither present, eliminating the crash window. The two fixes are complementary: the unique constraint handles concurrency, the single transaction handles crashes.

At National Bank of India, two consumer instances double-credited Priya because both passed the naive check, and separately a consumer credited her then crashed before marking, and the redelivery credited her again. The team first tried reordering the lines and it still double-processed, which taught everyone that the fix is atomicity, not ordering. The external-effect caveat is that emails and API calls cannot join the database transaction, so you record intent in an outbox and perform the external action idempotently afterward.

Remember one sentence: naive check-then-act dedup double-processes because the check and mark are separate, so fix it with an atomic INSERT under a UNIQUE constraint and commit the mark in the same transaction as the business change.
